prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms confined at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of Doppler and recoil shifts, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B041 as a single-part prize for Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Round 1 sharpened rather than weakened the case. Six of eight files now prefer it with an identical pair, the two files that prefer B017 list B041 as their first or second alternative, and nobody disputes the physics. The discovery is a specific physical insight, that a lattice at the magic wavelength makes the light shifts of the two clock levels cancel, so that many atoms can be held Doppler- and recoil-free and interrogated in parallel. That insight changed what can be measured: independently reproduced uncertainties near 10^-18, redshift resolved over millimetres, tighter limits on varying constants and on dark-matter couplings. In answer to the chair's first question, I would anchor the citation on the magic-wavelength lattice itself and name the lattice clock explicitly, so that the comb of 2005 appears at most as enabling technology and the 2012 single-ion control prize is not reprised. On Ye, the second question: his credit for this prize rests on bringing the lattice clock to the 10^-18 regime and on the many-body, spin-polarised Fermi-gas clock work that exposed and controlled its systematics. Both are lattice-clock achievements, and the comb programme is not needed to justify his name. Katori supplies the concept and the first realisations; Ye supplies the performance that made the concept a new class of instrument.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objections are three. First, this is a measurement invention, and a third precision-spectroscopy prize after 2005 and 2012 may look incremental; I do not accept that, because the many-atom regime is physically distinct from both earlier prizes, but I accept that the committee must say so in the citation. Second, two names cannot cover Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, who were decisive for individual accuracy milestones; the cut is imperfect, but those milestones refine a concept whose origin and first high-accuracy realisation are identifiable. Third, B017 has more field-creating novelty than a clock, and Olsson argues this outweighs clean attribution. I give B017 real weight, but the unresolved pairing mechanism, sample-to-sample variability and the exclusion of Cao and Fatemi from any three-name credit make me think it will be a stronger prize in a few years than it is now. I also note that I am a member of the AMO community and cannot judge the condensed-matter case as closely as Olsson or Eriksson.

responses.point: Pearce asks that the citation be anchored on the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, with the comb treated only as enabling technology, and asks how much of Ye's credit rests on the lattice clock rather than on the comb and broader clock programme.
responses.response: I agree with the anchoring and propose the wording above, which names the magic-wavelength condition and the Doppler- and recoil-free many-atom interrogation, the two features absent from the 2005 and 2012 citations. On Ye, I would not defend his name through comb-based spectroscopy at all. His claim here is the push of the lattice clock to 10^-18 and the many-body clock measurements that showed how to control collisional and density shifts; those are lattice-clock results. If the committee found that argument insufficient, the answer would be to reconsider the configuration, not to widen the citation to the comb. I also accept your instrumentalist point that the AMANDA-era and IceCube credit problem is real, and it is part of why I do not move to B029.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B017, judging that field-creating novelty outweighs the cleaner allocation of B041, and regards the clock as a refinement of a lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I take the novelty argument seriously, and moire materials are a new platform in a way a better clock is not. I still disagree on two points. The lineage claim holds for the comb and for single ions, but a magic-wavelength lattice with many atoms is a different regime and changed what can be measured, which is itself a criterion of the prize. And on timing, your own case against names the unresolved superconductivity mechanism, twist-angle inhomogeneity and the omitted experimental groups. Those weaknesses are real and are absent from B041. I would be content for B017 to be the next serious candidate, and I would rather see it recognised when the citation can be drawn without a hard cut around Cao, Fatemi and the hBN groups.

responses.point: Lindroth raises whether recognition would be more natural after a redefinition of the SI second, and how to weigh the many strontium and ytterbium groups against the two credited names.
responses.response: On timing, I hold that the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows from the physics and should not govern a physics prize; independent clocks agree at the 10^-18 level now, and waiting would reward bureaucratic scheduling over scientific maturity. I recognise that you and Pearce read the same fact as an argument for timing, and I have no objection to noting the redefinition in the discussion. On the many groups, I agree it is the strongest argument against a narrow credit. My answer is the citation: it is drawn on the concept and its record-setting realisation, so later accuracy records and the Paris, PTB and NIST systematics work are refinements. Your point on blackbody-radiation shifts is useful, since it confirms that the physics is soundly understood and not a single demonstration.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B017 with an emphasis on the prediction and observed phases, and would accept B041 prevailing if maturity is judged decisive.
responses.response: I appreciate that you would accept B041 on maturity grounds, and I think maturity is decisive here for the reasons you have in part shared, namely the unsettled mechanism. I would not argue that B041 is a more important discovery in all senses than B017, only that it is the better-documented one for this year, and that each member's weight on novelty versus certainty is the honest difference between us. I also note that I cannot evaluate your first alternative, altermagnetism, with expertise, so I do not rank it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the boundary against the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize as drawn in the proposed citation, or wants a wider clock citation that would add other laboratories and require more than three names.
How much weight members who stress invention versus discovery will place on B041 relative to B017; I regard that as a genuine difference in criteria, not a factual disagreement I can resolve.
Whether early proposers of lattice trapping or later accuracy-record groups have a claim that two names cannot capture. I rely on the supplied credit and on memory for priority details.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure, in answer to the chair's seventh question. My doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, the JILA environment from which Ye's work grew. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, and I have no personal or institutional tie to either. I work in the same broad atomic and quantum-optics community as several candidates, including those on B002, also without a documented collaboration. I do not believe any of this requires recusal on B041 or B017, and I would accept the committee's decision if it judged otherwise. I defer to colleagues on whether the Boulder stay matters; I have not relied on it in my argument.
